guide.title: Ponte, Rome: the bridge the rione is named for, Palazzo Altemps and via dei Coronari
guide.intro: Ponte is the fifth of Rome's twenty-two rioni by toponymic code, and it takes both its name and its coat of arms from a bridge: Ponte Sant'Angelo, which the rione's arms show white on a red field. It is a small, densely built wedge of the left bank between the Tiber and corso Vittorio Emanuele II, and its plan is still medieval. Via dei Coronari runs straight through it because it was the pilgrims' road toward St Peter's; Monte Giordano, the low rise the Orsini fortified, carries Palazzo Taverna on top of it. Ponte holds Santa Maria della Pace with Bramante's cloister behind it, Santa Maria dell'Anima, the Renaissance palace that is now the Museo Nazionale Romano at Palazzo Altemps, the Florentine national church at the head of via Giulia, and three of the bridges that cross toward the Vatican side. The embankment roads built after 1870 erased the lanes that once ran down to the water.

sections.heading: The rione's edges
sections.body:
Ponte's landward edge is a set of streets and squares it shares with Parione, and Roma Capitale's own street register says so in terms: via del Governo Vecchio, via della Pace, via di Santa Maria dell'Anima, via di Tor Sanguigna, piazza di Tor Sanguigna, piazza del Fico and largo Febo are all recorded as lying in Ponte and in Parione together. The same register records piazza Navona as Parione alone, and corso Vittorio Emanuele II in four rioni at once.

Where a street is shared, a building on it belongs to the rione it physically stands in, not to the whole length of the street it is addressed on. Santa Maria dell'Anima, Palazzo Sacchetti, San Biagio degli Armeni and Santa Maria del Suffragio stand in Ponte, while the streets they are addressed on lie in more than one rione. Via Giulia was opened in 1508 and runs 950 metres from piazza San Vincenzo Pallotti to piazza dell'Oro. Its southern length lies in Regola; its northern length lies in Rione V Ponte.

The bridges divide too. Ponte Sant'Angelo and Ponte Vittorio Emanuele II each lie in Ponte and in Borgo; Ponte Umberto I lies in Ponte and in Prati.

sections.heading: Getting there
sections.body:
No source states a metro station or a bus route for these addresses, so none is given here, and neither are walking times or any distance this guide has not taken from a source. Steer by addresses instead; the whole rione uses the postcode 00186.

Roma Capitale gives the Museo Nazionale Romano at Palazzo Altemps as Via di Sant'Apollinare, 46, and notes that the front on via di Sant'Apollinare carries the main entrance. It gives Santa Maria della Pace and the Chiostro del Bramante as Arco della Pace, 5, which is the small street behind the church front. Santi Celso e Giuliano in Banchi is at Vicolo del Curato, 12, and not on via del Banco di Santo Spirito, where its front stands. San Giovanni Battista dei Fiorentini is at Via Acciaioli, 2, at the head of via Giulia. The Oratorio del Gonfalone is at Via del Gonfalone, 32a. The sanctuary of San Salvatore in Lauro and the museums of the Pio Sodalizio dei Piceni share the number 15 on Piazza di San Salvatore in Lauro but keep separate telephone numbers and separate hours.

Via dei Coronari runs from piazza di Tor Sanguigna to piazza dei Coronari and is about 500 metres long. Via Paola runs from piazza dell'Oro to piazza di Ponte Sant'Angelo, which is the walk from the Florentine church to the bridgehead.

sections.heading: Opening hours, and where there are none
sections.body:
Four places in Ponte publish clock times. Roma Capitale gives the Museo Nazionale Romano at Palazzo Altemps as Tuesday to Sunday 09.30 to 19.00, last admission 18.00, closed Monday. It gives the Museo Napoleonico as Tuesday to Sunday 10.00 to 18.00, last entry 17.15, with 10.00 to 14.00 on 24 and 31 December. It gives the Musei di San Salvatore in Lauro as Tuesday to Saturday 10.00 to 13.00 and 16.00 to 19.00, closed Sunday and Monday. And it gives Santi Celso e Giuliano in Banchi as 07.00 to 12.00 and 15.00 to 19.00 on weekdays, 08.00 to 13.30 and 15.00 to 19.45 on feast days, adding that times may vary.

San Giovanni Battista dei Fiorentini publishes two sets, one for winter and one for July and August, and Roma Capitale asks visitors to contact the church because times may vary. The Chiostro del Bramante is an exhibition venue whose hours change with the show: Roma Capitale states that the ticket office is open every day and closes one hour before the venue, and directs readers to chiostrodelbramante.it for current times.

Everywhere else in this guide, no source states opening hours, so none are given. That includes Santa Maria della Pace, Santa Maria dell'Anima, San Biagio degli Armeni, Santa Maria del Suffragio and the Museo Mario Praz. For Santa Maria della Pace, Roma Capitale gives the telephone number 06 68804038 and says to contact the church about mass times and visiting. For the Oratorio del Gonfalone it gives the telephone number 06 6875952 and the addresses direzioneartistica@oratoriogonfalone.eu and info@oratoriogonfalone.eu, and says to use them to arrange a visit. None of the palazzi in this guide publishes hours, and none of them should be assumed to admit visitors.

faq.question: Is Ponte Sant'Angelo in the rione Ponte?
faq.answer: Partly, and the rione is named after it. it.wikipedia's article on the rione says the bridge lies in Ponte and in Borgo, and that it belonged to the rione until Sixtus V created Borgo in the sixteenth century. The same article gives the rione's arms, citing Carlo Pietrangeli, as the bridge of Sant'Angelo white on a red field. Ponte Vittorio Emanuele II divides the same way; Ponte Umberto I is shared with Prati.

faq.question: Is via Giulia in Ponte?
faq.answer: Its northern length is. Via Giulia was opened in 1508 and runs 950 metres from piazza San Vincenzo Pallotti to piazza dell'Oro. Its southern length lies in Regola; its northern length lies in Rione V Ponte. The buildings on its northern length that stand inside Ponte are Palazzo Sacchetti at no. 66, San Biagio degli Armeni and Santa Maria del Suffragio.

faq.question: Which museums in Ponte can you actually walk into?
faq.answer: Four publish times. The Museo Nazionale Romano at Palazzo Altemps opens Tuesday to Sunday 09.30 to 19.00 with last admission at 18.00. The Museo Napoleonico, a Roma Capitale civic museum in Palazzo Primoli, opens Tuesday to Sunday 10.00 to 18.00 with last entry at 17.15. The Musei di San Salvatore in Lauro open Tuesday to Saturday 10.00 to 13.00 and 16.00 to 19.00 and close Sunday and Monday. The Chiostro del Bramante runs exhibitions whose hours change with the show, so Roma Capitale directs readers to the venue's own site. The Museo Mario Praz shares Palazzo Primoli with the Museo Napoleonico, but no source states its opening hours, so none are given here.

faq.question: Is piazza Navona in Ponte?
faq.answer: No. Roma Capitale's street register records piazza Navona in Parione alone. The line between the two rioni runs through the streets immediately behind the square, several of which the same register records as lying in both. Santa Maria della Pace, Santa Maria dell'Anima and the Chiostro del Bramante stand on the Ponte side of that line.

faq.question: Can you go inside the palazzi?
faq.answer: Assume not. No source states visiting hours for Palazzo Sacchetti, Palazzo Taverna, Palazzo Lancellotti, Palazzo Cesi-Gaddi, Palazzo Milesi, Palazzo Alberini, Palazzo Boncompagni Corcos, Palazzo Capponi Stampa or the Casa di Fiammetta, so none are given here, and Roma Capitale's page for Palazzo Sacchetti gives none either. Two palace interiors in Ponte are open on museum terms rather than as palaces: Palazzo Altemps, which holds the Museo Nazionale Romano, and Palazzo Primoli, which holds the Museo Napoleonico and the Museo Mario Praz.

faq.question: What was the Tor di Nona?
faq.answer: A tower on the river bank that gave its name to a lungotevere, a theatre and a set of prisons. it.wikipedia records that the tower passed to the hospital of the Compagnia del Salvatore in 1395 under the will of Giovanni di Jacobello Orsini, and that the name probably comes from its being the ninth tower counting from Porta Flaminia. From the early fifteenth century the prisons there and those of Corte Savella were together called the presone dello papa, a name they kept until 1657. Nothing of the prisons survives. The Teatro Tordinona on via degli Acquasparta carries forward the name of the Teatro Apollo-Tordinona, which stood on the prison site and was demolished in 1888.

photos.title: Ponte Sant'Angelo
photos.description: Ponte Sant'Angelo across the Tiber, showing the three main arches of Hadrian's pons Aelius of 136 AD and the angel statues set along its parapet in 1668.
photos.author: John Samuel

places.name: Ponte Sant'Angelo
places.summary: The pedestrian bridge that gives the rione its name and its coat of arms. It lies in two rioni, Ponte on the left bank and Borgo on the right. it.wikipedia's article on the rione records that the bridge belonged to the rione until Sixtus V created Borgo in the sixteenth century, and gives the arms, citing Carlo Pietrangeli, as the bridge of Sant'Angelo white on a red field.
places.history: Roma Capitale records that Hadrian had it built in 136 AD as the pons Aelius, to link his mausoleum to the city. It is peperino faced with travertine, with three arches, approached by ramps carried on three minor arches on the left bank and two on the right; the right-bank ramp arches were destroyed in 1893 for the embankment works and replaced with modern ones. Ricimer's Gothic troops used the bridge in July 472. In 1668 ten statues of angels bearing the symbols of the Passion were added. Roma Capitale records that Bernini designed the figures at Clement IX's commission and entrusted their execution to his pupils.

places.name: Museo Nazionale Romano - Palazzo Altemps
places.summary: One of the four sites of the Museo Nazionale Romano, in a Renaissance palace whose main entrance Roma Capitale places on via di Sant'Apollinare. Roma Capitale gives the hours as Tuesday to Sunday 09.30 to 19.00, last admission 18.00, closed Monday, and the telephone number 06 684851. The Boncompagni Ludovisi collection shown here comprised about 450 sculptures, of which the State acquired 104; fifteen of Cardinal Altemps's original 120 survive, four of them under the north portico. The palace chapel of Sant'Aniceto held the relics of Pope Anicetus, 155 to 166, found in the catacombs of San Callisto and granted by Clement VIII in 1603. A small theatre named for Goldoni is inside the palace.
places.history: Roma Capitale records that the palace was raised in 1477 for Girolamo Riario, duke of Imola and nephew of Sixtus IV, over earlier medieval buildings, and that Melozzo da Forli, Luca Pacioli and perhaps Leon Battista Alberti took part in its construction. It was sold in 1511 to Cardinal Francesco Soderini and later became Cardinal Innocenzo Cybo's residence. Cardinal Marco Sittico Altemps bought it in 1568 and had Martino Longhi the Elder remodel it between 1577 and 1595, including the altana toward piazza Sant'Apollinare under four pyramidal spires and a dome topped by the Altemps rampant ram. Giacomo Della Porta, Flaminio Ponzio, Tommaso Schiratti, Girolamo Rainaldi and Onorio Longhi also worked there. In 1887 the palace became property of the Holy See and housed the Pontifical Spanish College; the Italian State bought it in 1982.

places.name: Chiesa di Santa Maria della Pace
places.summary: The church behind the small trapezoidal square west of piazza Navona, with Pietro da Cortona's convex front of 1656, made for Alexander VII Chigi. No source states its opening hours, so none are given here; Roma Capitale gives the telephone number 06 68804038 and says to contact the church about mass times and visiting.
places.history: Roma Capitale records that the church stands where Sant'Andrea de Acquarenariis stood, named for the water-sellers who drew from the Tiber and settled out the sand. By tradition, in 1480 the image of the Virgin under the portico bled after a drunken soldier threw a stone at it, and Sixtus IV renamed the church Santa Maria della Virtu; it was later named Santa Maria della Pace for the Peace of Bagnolo, which ended the war between the Papal State, Venice and the Kingdom of Naples. The dome was added in 1524 to Antonio da Sangallo the Younger's design and Carlo Maderno's altar dates from 1614. The Sibyls and angels on the chapel arch are Raphael's, 1514, and the four Prophets above were finished to his design by Timoteo Viti.

places.name: Chiostro del Bramante
places.summary: Bramante's cloister for Santa Maria della Pace, now an exhibition venue. Roma Capitale states that the exhibition ticket office is open every day and closes one hour before the venue, and directs readers to the official site, chiostrodelbramante.it, for current times; the telephone number is 06 68809035. The cloister and the church physically adjoin, and from the first floor there is a view of Raphael's Sibyls in the church.
places.history: it.wikipedia records that Cardinal Oliviero Carafa commissioned the cloister around 1500 and that Donato Bramante designed it, and that it was built between 1500 and 1504. The square plan is generated by repeating a module equal to the width of the portico, giving a central void four modules by four and a refectory two by four; sixteen piers carry a continuous cross-vaulted portico, and the elevation has two orders proportioned to the Vitruvian rule. The lunettes on the back wall are frescoed with Stories of the Life of the Virgin. It became an exhibition space and cultural centre in 1996, run by DART - Chiostro del Bramante.

places.name: Chiesa di Santa Maria dell'Anima
places.address: Via di Santa Maria dell'Anima, 66, 00186 Roma RM
places.summary: The national church of the German-speaking Catholic community in Rome, on a street that Roma Capitale's register records as lying in both Ponte and Parione; the building itself stands in Ponte. No source states its opening hours, so none are given here.
places.history: it.wikipedia records that the church was founded in the fourteenth century as the oratory of the German hospice, that the rebuilding was decided on for the Jubilee of 1500 and that the new church was consecrated in 1542. Johannes Burckardt, a member of the confraternity from 1489 and later its provost, wanted a northern European plan with side aisles the same height as the nave. The facade is by Andrea Sansovino, completed by Giuliano da Sangallo, and the campanile is attributed to Bramante. The funerary monument of Pope Adrian VI was made between 1524 and 1527 by Angelo di Mariano, called Michelangelo Senese, to a design by Baldassarre Peruzzi, at the commission of Cardinal Willem Enckenwoirt. The church was sacked under the Napoleonic occupation and its sacristy used as a stable; a seminary was instituted here in 1859.

places.name: Basilica di San Giovanni Battista dei Fiorentini
places.summary: The Florentine national church, at the head of via Giulia. Roma Capitale gives winter hours of Monday to Friday 08.30 to 11.30 and 17.30 to 19.00, Sundays and feast days 08.30 to 13.00 and 17.30 to 19.00; and for July and August, Monday to Friday 08.30 to 12.00 and 17.00 to 19.00, Sundays and feast days 08.30 to 13.00 and 17.30 to 20.00. It notes that times may vary and asks visitors to contact the church. The telephone number is 06 68892059.
places.history: Roma Capitale records that Leo X held a competition for the church in 1518, entered by Raphael, Michelangelo and Peruzzi among others, and that Jacopo Sansovino's project won; the interior was completed only in 1620, through Antonio da Sangallo the Younger, Giacomo Della Porta and Carlo Maderno, who worked here in 1614 and raised the elongated dome the Romans call il confetto succhiato. The travertine facade with six Florentine saints is Alessandro Galilei's, 1734, under Clement XII, and the church was restored in 1992. Borromini and Maderno are buried here; Bernini's busts of Antonio Coppola and Antonio Cepparelli are held here; Ferdinando Fuga made the chapel of San Filippo Neri, who was rector from 1564 to 1575. it.wikipedia records a museum of sacred art at the same address holding works the basilica acquired over the centuries, and that the Florentine oratory of Sant'Orsola della Pieta, which stood where the western end of corso Vittorio Emanuele II now runs, belongs to the same story. No source states the museum's opening hours, so none are given here.

places.name: Basilica dei Santi Celso e Giuliano in Banchi
places.summary: The church of the Banchi, the papal banking quarter, whose front stands on via del Banco di Santo Spirito while Roma Capitale gives its address on vicolo del Curato. Roma Capitale gives the hours as 07.00 to 12.00 and 15.00 to 19.00 on weekdays, and 08.00 to 13.30 and 15.00 to 19.45 on feast days, adding that times may vary.
places.history: Roma Capitale records that the church was consecrated in 432 by Pope Celestine I and enlarged in the ninth century; that Innocent III made it a papal chapel in 1198; that it was rebuilt in the sixteenth century and restored in the nineteenth; and that it holds the dignity of a minor basilica.

places.name: Santuario di San Salvatore in Lauro
places.address: Piazza di San Salvatore in Lauro, 15, 00186 Roma RM
places.summary: The working sanctuary on the square of the same name, sharing a street number with the museums of the Pio Sodalizio dei Piceni but keeping its own telephone number, 066875187. Roma Capitale says to consult the official site or to telephone for mass and service times, so no clock times are given here. it.wikipedia records it as the national church of the Marchigiani in Rome and the seat of the diaconate of the same name.
places.history: Roma Capitale records that, according to some historical documentation, the first church here was founded by the Tiber around the year 1000 by a small order of monks, and was destroyed in barbarian raids; that it was rebuilt and enlarged in 1177 by the Celestines, devoted to San Giorgio in Alga, who held it about two hundred years; and that in 1668, after their suppression, it passed to the Pio Sodalizio dei Piceni, which instituted the cult of the Madonna di Loreto here.

places.name: Musei di San Salvatore in Lauro
places.address: Piazza di San Salvatore in Lauro, 15, 00186 Roma RM
places.summary: The museums inside the monumental complex held by the Pio Sodalizio dei Piceni, at the same street number as the sanctuary but with their own hours and telephone. Roma Capitale gives the hours as Tuesday to Saturday 10.00 to 13.00 and 16.00 to 19.00, closed Sunday and Monday, and the telephone number 06 6875608. It records that the museums house the permanent donations and galleries of Emilio Greco and Umberto Mastroianni, and that they have shown Visioni del Grand Tour dall'Ermitage, the Gogol bicentenary, Dostoevskij e l'Italia, Cinetismo and the Francesco Messina centenary.
places.history: it.wikipedia records that the Pio Sodalizio dei Piceni grew from an association formed at the start of the seventeenth century at the instance of Cardinal Gianbattista Pallotta of Caldarola, and that Urban VIII made it the Confraternita della Santa Casa di Loreto in 1633. The feast of the Piceni is kept in Rome on 10 December each year, the anniversary of the translation of the Holy House.

places.name: Basilica di Sant'Apollinare
places.summary: A church of ancient foundation standing against Palazzo Apollinare, which houses the Pontificia Universita della Santa Croce. No source states its opening hours, so none are given here.
places.history: it.wikipedia records that Pope Hadrian I founded the church around 780 on Roman remains, that it is first recorded in his life in the Liber pontificalis and again in the tenth-century chronicle of Benedetto del Soratte, and that it holds the dignity of a minor basilica.

places.name: Oratorio del Gonfalone
places.summary: The oratory of the Arciconfraternita del Gonfalone, used for concerts and home to the Coro Polifonico Romano. No source states its opening hours, so none are given here; Roma Capitale gives the telephone number 06 6875952 and the addresses direzioneartistica@oratoriogonfalone.eu and info@oratoriogonfalone.eu, and says to use them to arrange a visit.
places.history: Roma Capitale records that the oratory was built between 1544 and 1547 over the church of Santa Lucia Vecchia for the Arciconfraternita del Gonfalone, whose origins go back to the thirteenth century and whose Compagnia was officially recognised by a Breve of Clement IV in 1267. The two-order facade is by Domenico Castelli. The rectangular sixteenth-century interior carries a Storie della Passione di Cristo cycle in twelve episodes, from the entry into Jerusalem to the Resurrection, painted between 1569 and 1576 by Federico Zuccari, Cesare Nebbia and Livio Agresti, under a carved wooden ceiling of 1568 by Ambrogio Bonazzini. it.wikipedia records that the adjoining Palazzo del Gonfalone, between via del Gonfalone and via Giulia, was the juvenile prison established by Leo XII in 1827.

places.name: Chiesa di Santa Maria del Suffragio
places.summary: A seventeenth-century church on the northern length of via Giulia, which lies in Ponte. No source states its opening hours, so none are given here.
places.history: it.wikipedia records that the confraternity del Suffragio was founded in 1592 at San Biagio della Pagnotta to pray for the dead, approved by Clement VIII in 1594 and raised to an arciconfraternita by Paul V in 1620, and that from 1607 it acquired part of the site originally meant for Bramante's Palazzo dei Tribunali.

places.name: Chiesa di San Biagio degli Armeni
places.summary: The Armenian Catholic church in Rome, on the northern length of via Giulia, in the block of Palazzo Sacchetti. No source states its opening hours, so none are given here.
places.history: it.wikipedia records that the nickname della Pagnotta comes from the small blessed loaves distributed on St Blaise's day, 3 February, and that medieval documents give a string of variant names traceable to de cantu secuta.

places.name: Chiesa dei Santi Simone e Giuda
places.address: Via di San Simone, 00186 Roma RM
places.summary: A deconsecrated medieval church at the top of a flight of steps on via di San Simone. It cannot be entered.
places.history: it.wikipedia records a twelfth-century building consecrated by Paschal II, who reigned from 1099 to 1118, and again by Innocent II in 1143, whose inscription survives in the fabric. It was originally Santa Maria in Monticellis, after Monte Giordano, and took the apostles' dedication only from the middle of the sixteenth century. It was deconsecrated in 1902 and afterwards divided into housing, the Alcazar cinema, a restaurant, and finally a theatre, the Teatro dei Coronari, which has been closed since 2006.

places.name: Museo Napoleonico
places.summary: A Roma Capitale civic museum of Napoleonic material on the ground floor of Palazzo Primoli. Roma Capitale gives the hours as Tuesday to Sunday 10.00 to 18.00, last entry 17.15, with 10.00 to 14.00 on 24 and 31 December, and the telephone number 060608. it.wikipedia records that the collection came chiefly from Count Giuseppe Primoli, 1851 to 1927, son of Carlotta Bonaparte and so a descendant of the family, and that he gave it to the city of Rome in 1927.
places.history: Roma Capitale records that the palace dates from the sixteenth century. It belonged to the Gottifredi, a holding still marked on Nolli's plan of 1748, and passed to the Filonardi at the end of the eighteenth century. Count Luigi Primoli bought it between 1820 and 1828. After the Tiber embankment walls and the opening of via Zanardelli reshaped the area, Count Giuseppe Primoli, sole owner from 1901, entrusted the rebuilding to the architect Raffaele Ojetti: the old front on piazza dell'Orso came down, a new block with corner loggias went up, a monumental entrance was made on via Zanardelli, the building was raised, and a new facade was given to piazza di Ponte Umberto. The work finished in 1911.

places.name: Museo Mario Praz
places.summary: A house-museum on the third floor of Palazzo Primoli, in the same building as the Museo Napoleonico but under a different owner. No source states its opening hours, so none are given here.
places.history: Roma Capitale records that the museum has occupied the third floor since 1 June 1995, that it belongs to the Galleria Nazionale d'Arte Moderna, and that it holds about a thousand works - furniture, paintings, drawings, terracottas, bronzes, miniatures, silver, from the late eighteenth century to the first half of the nineteenth - collected by the anglicist and art critic Mario Praz, 1896 to 1982.

places.name: Teatro Tordinona
places.summary: A working theatre on via degli Acquasparta, also called the Sala Pirandello. No source states its programme or its opening times, so none are given here.
places.history: it.wikipedia records that the theatre carries the name of the Teatro Apollo-Tordinona, demolished in 1888, which arose in 1670 at the wish of Christina of Sweden. She asked her secretary, Count Giacomo d'Alibert, to obtain from Clement IX a building formerly Orsini property on what is now lungotevere Tor di Nona, which had been used as a prison until 1657.

places.name: L'Arciliuto
places.summary: A small theatre housed in Palazzo Montevecchio Chiovenda, on piazza di Montevecchio. No programme or opening times are given here.
places.history: No source states its history, so none is given here.

places.name: Palazzo Sacchetti
places.summary: A late Renaissance palace on the northern length of via Giulia, which lies in Ponte. No source states its visiting hours, so none are given here, and the interior should not be assumed open.
places.history: Roma Capitale records that Antonio da Sangallo the Younger, 1483 to 1546, designed and built the palace and lived in it; the inscription to the left of the balcony reads Domus Antonii Sangalli Architecti - MDXLIII. On Sangallo's death it was sold to the Ricci di Montepulciano, who had Nanni di Baccio Bigio restructure and enlarge it, and it was sold to the Marchesi Sacchetti in 1648. The Salone dell'Udienza carries Francesco Salviati's Storie di David, 1553 to 1554; the Salone dei mappamondi holds two late seventeenth-century globes by the cosmographer Vincenzo Coronelli; the Galleria has Pietro da Cortona's Sacra Famiglia and Adamo ed Eva; and a sixteenth-century fountain with a putto between dolphins stands at the corner with vicolo del Cefalo.

places.name: Palazzo Taverna
places.address: Via di Monte Giordano, 00186 Roma RM
places.summary: The palace that stands on Monte Giordano, also known as Palazzo Orsini Taverna and formerly Palazzo Gabrielli. Monte Giordano is a small rise in the centre of Rome, in the Regio formerly called Scorteclaria, probably formed by the accumulation of debris from the ancient river landing at Tor di Nona.
places.history: it.wikipedia records that the palace was built for Cardinal Giordano Orsini on his fortress on Monte Giordano; that it was later let to Cardinal Ippolito II d'Este, who hosted Torquato Tasso there, and to Cardinal Maurizio of Savoy; and that it passed to the Gabrielli in 1688, who hosted members of the Bonaparte family, among them the Empress Eugenie and Cardinal Luciano-Luigi, who died there. The hill itself is known from the middle of the twelfth century as a fortified holding of Johannes Roncionis, and a bull of Alexander III of 1177 attests the church of Santa Maria in Monticello on it, belonging to the monastery of Sant'Elia di Falleri. In the following century it belonged to Stefano Petri de Monte, of the Stefaneschi, who held the Turris Maior on it. The Orsini took possession progressively between 1242 and 1262, and the hill is named after an Orsini Giordano.

places.name: Palazzo del Banco di Santo Spirito
places.address: Via del Banco di Santo Spirito, 00186 Roma RM
places.summary: The former papal mint, the Zecca Vecchia, which gives the street its name and stands at the heart of the Banchi quarter.
places.history: it.wikipedia records that Julius II ordered a monetary reform in 1504 and gave Bramante the job of adapting an existing building as the papal mint. The silver giulii, worth a tenth of the gold ducat, were struck here, along with coins and medals, some of them the work of Benvenuto Cellini. Leo X had Antonio da Sangallo the Younger build the facade, completed in 1524, whose slightly concave form drew comment.

places.name: Palazzo Alberini
places.address: Via del Banco di Santo Spirito, 12, 00186 Roma RM
places.summary: A Renaissance palace in the Banchi, also known as Palazzo Cicciaporci. Its present facade is nineteenth-century.
places.history: it.wikipedia records that the palace was built for Giulio Alberini between 1515 and 1519 and completed in 1521 by Pietro Rosselli. Its design is not settled: the article attributes it to Raphael, notes that Vasari says Giulio Romano designed it for him, and attributes the ground floor to Bramante, possibly in 1512.

places.name: Palazzo Lancellotti
places.summary: The Lancellotti family palace, on the square and street that carry the family's name.
places.history: it.wikipedia records that the palace was begun in 1591 to Francesco da Volterra's design for Cardinal Scipione Lancellotti and completed for Cardinal Orazio Lancellotti by Carlo Maderno in 1610. Its frescoes were finished later under Agostino Tassi, among them the Sala dei Palafrenieri, and the portal is by Domenichino. It was the first seat of the Circolo San Pietro, founded in 1869.

places.name: Palazzo Cesi-Gaddi
places.address: Via della Maschera d'Oro, 00186 Roma RM
places.summary: A sixteenth-century palace at the corner of via della Maschera d'Oro and via degli Acquasparta.
places.history: it.wikipedia records that the Gaddi, Florentine merchants, built it in the early sixteenth century and that it was sold to the Rossi di San Secondo, then in 1567 to Angelo Cesi. In 1570 it was let to Ugo Boncompagni, who was Gregory XIII from 1572, and afterwards returned to the Cesi. Federico Cesi, duke of Acquasparta, lived here.

places.name: Palazzo Milesi
places.address: Via della Maschera d'Oro, 9, 00186 Roma RM
places.summary: The palace that gave via della Maschera d'Oro its name, from a sixteenth-century golden-mask fresco once at the centre of its facade, now lost.
places.history: it.wikipedia records a fifteenth-century origin and that the palace was built by the Milesi, a family from Bergamo: Giovanni Giuseppe Milesi moved to Rome in 1480 and had it put up in the early 1500s, possibly by joining three separate houses.

places.name: Palazzo Montevecchio Chiovenda
places.summary: A Renaissance palace on piazza di Montevecchio, which houses the Arciliuto.
places.history: it.wikipedia records that it was probably built for the counts, later dukes, of Montevecchio, a branch of the Gabrielli of Gubbio, and that it was finished around 1515. The design is attributed to Baldassarre Peruzzi without documentary certainty. The same article carries, as a tradition rather than as a fact, the story that Raphael first lodged here.

places.name: Palazzo Boncompagni Corcos
places.summary: A Mannerist palace at the corner of via degli Orsini, facing piazza dell'Orologio. It is also known as Palazzo Scarinci.
places.history: it.wikipedia records that in 1582 Salomon Corcos, educated by the Oratorians, converted and took the name of the reigning pope, Ugo Boncompagni, Gregory XIII, and that the family was then able to build this palace in the seventeenth century. It later belonged to the Scarinci and to the Camerata.

places.name: Palazzo Capponi Stampa
places.address: Via dei Banchi Nuovi, 00186 Roma RM
places.summary: A seventeenth-century palace at the corner of via dei Banchi Nuovi and via degli Orsini, also known as Palazzo Orsini Capponi Stampa Pediconi.
places.history: it.wikipedia records that it was built in the early 1600s for Cosimo Orsini, sold in 1672 to Monsignor Capponi, bishop of Mileto, and passed to the Stampa in the eighteenth century.

places.name: Casa di Fiammetta
places.summary: A Renaissance house on the small square that carries its owner's name, at the corner of via della Maschera d'Oro and via degli Acquasparta.
places.history: it.wikipedia records that the house belonged to Fiammetta Michaelis, the Florentine courtesan and favourite of the humanist Cardinal Giacomo Ammannati Piccolomini, and that she inherited the cardinal's estate on his death in 1479 - a bequest Sixtus IV blocked, appointing a commission.

places.name: Via dei Coronari
places.summary: The straight street that runs through the middle of the rione, from piazza di Tor Sanguigna to piazza dei Coronari, about 500 metres long. Roma Capitale's street register records it, and piazza dei Coronari with it, as lying in Ponte alone. Its frontage today is antique dealers and small shops.
places.history: it.wikipedia records that the street is medieval in origin and was called Via Recta for its regular alignment, and that it served as a route from the Porto di Ripetta toward St Peter's. It was heavily used by pilgrims, and so by the sellers of corone - rosaries - and of holy images, who set up their shops along it and gave the street its name. From the early sixteenth century the street and its surroundings were lived in by some of the city's higher-ranking courtesans.

places.name: Via Paola
places.summary: The street that joins the head of via Giulia to the bridgehead of Ponte Sant'Angelo. Roma Capitale's street register records it as running from piazza dell'Oro to piazza di Ponte Sant'Angelo, and as lying in Ponte alone.
places.history: No source states its history, so none is given here. It is the connection between San Giovanni Battista dei Fiorentini, at the via Acciaioli end of via Giulia, and the square at the bridge.

places.name: Via dei Banchi Nuovi
places.address: Via dei Banchi Nuovi, 00186 Roma RM
places.summary: One of the two streets of the Banchi, the papal banking quarter that gives Santi Celso e Giuliano in Banchi the second half of its name. Roma Capitale's street register records it as lying in Ponte alone. Palazzo Capponi Stampa stands at its corner with via degli Orsini.
places.history: No source states its history beyond the banking quarter it belongs to, so none is given here.

places.name: Via del Banco di Santo Spirito
places.address: Via del Banco di Santo Spirito, 00186 Roma RM
places.summary: The Banchi street named after the palace of the Banco di Santo Spirito, the former papal mint, which stands on it. Palazzo Alberini is at no. 12, and the front of Santi Celso e Giuliano in Banchi stands on this street although the church is addressed on vicolo del Curato. Roma Capitale's street register records it as lying in Ponte alone.
places.history: No source states its history beyond the buildings on it, so none is given here.

places.name: Via della Maschera d'Oro
places.address: Via della Maschera d'Oro, 00186 Roma RM
places.summary: A street of painted and decorated fronts. Palazzo Milesi, Palazzo Cesi-Gaddi and the Casa di Fiammetta all stand on it or at its corners. Roma Capitale's street register records it as lying in Ponte alone.
places.history: it.wikipedia records that the street is named from a sixteenth-century golden-mask fresco once at the centre of Palazzo Milesi's facade, now lost.

places.name: Via di Monte Giordano
places.address: Via di Monte Giordano, 00186 Roma RM
places.summary: The street that climbs Monte Giordano, the low rise carrying Palazzo Taverna. Roma Capitale's street register records it as lying in Ponte alone.
places.history: it.wikipedia records that Monte Giordano was probably formed by the accumulation of debris from the ancient river landing at Tor di Nona, that it is known from the middle of the twelfth century as a fortified holding, and that the Orsini took possession of it progressively between 1242 and 1262, giving it the name of an Orsini Giordano.

places.name: Via di Panico
places.summary: The other approach to Monte Giordano, running through the block between via dei Coronari and the Banchi. Roma Capitale's street register records it as lying in Ponte alone.
places.history: No source states its history, so none is given here.

places.name: Piazza di Ponte Sant'Angelo
places.address: Piazza di Ponte Sant'Angelo, 00186 Roma RM
places.summary: The square at the left-bank head of Ponte Sant'Angelo. Roma Capitale's street register records the square as lying in Ponte alone, although the bridge itself lies in two rioni.
places.history: it.wikipedia's article on the rione records that condemned prisoners were led here in procession and that a gallows stood in this square. The prisons that supplied it, the Carceri di Tor di Nona, stood along what is now lungotevere Tor di Nona and have left nothing standing.

places.name: Piazza di San Salvatore in Lauro
places.address: Piazza di San Salvatore in Lauro, 00186 Roma RM
places.summary: The square in front of the sanctuary of San Salvatore in Lauro and the monumental complex of the Pio Sodalizio dei Piceni, both at no. 15. Roma Capitale's street register records the square as lying in Ponte alone.
places.history: No source states the square's own history apart from the buildings on it, so none is given here.

places.name: Piazza dell'Orologio
places.summary: The square named after the clock on the tower of the Filippini convent, which stands over it. Palazzo Boncompagni Corcos and Palazzo Capponi Stampa both face it. Roma Capitale's street register records the square as lying in Ponte and in Parione. The Filippini convent itself is in Parione.
places.history: it.wikipedia records that Francesco Borromini built the clock tower in 1648 and that a Pietro da Cortona mosaic of the Madonna della Vallicella sits below the dial. Palazzo Bennicelli, on the square, was begun in 1660 to Borromini's design for Monsignor Virginio Spada, for the Banco di Santo Spirito.

places.name: Lungotevere Tor di Nona
places.address: Lungotevere Tor di Nona, 00186 Roma RM
places.summary: The embankment road along Ponte's river front, running from the square at Ponte Sant'Angelo to piazza di Ponte Umberto I. it.wikipedia records that it was instituted by a deliberation of 20 July 1887. The embankment roads built after 1870 erased the lanes that used to run down to the water, which is why the rione's older character survives further inland.
places.history: it.wikipedia records that the Carceri di Tor di Nona stood along this stretch, in a tower that passed to the hospital of the Compagnia del Salvatore in 1395 under the will of Giovanni di Jacobello Orsini, and that the name probably comes from its being the ninth tower counting from Porta Flaminia; the tower was anciently part of the city's defensive wall. From the early fifteenth century those prisons and the prisons of Corte Savella were together called the presone dello papa, a name they kept until 1657. The same source records that from Augustus' time the ground about 160 metres upstream of the Pons Aelius held one of Rome's two marble ports and the statio rationis marmorum, the imperial quarry-monopoly office; that landing was found in 1891, recorded, and destroyed during the building of the embankment walls.

places.name: Tor Sanguigna
places.summary: A medieval tower in Ponte, what survives of the stronghold of the Sanguigni family. The square in front of it is recorded by Roma Capitale's street register as lying in two rioni; the tower itself is in Ponte.
places.history: it.wikipedia records that the Sanguigni lived here until at least the fifteenth century and died out in the eighteenth, and that the tower possibly descends from a first tower built by the Gemini family before the eleventh century. In the Middle Ages the toponym covered the whole area between what is now via Zanardelli, via dei Coronari and Sant'Agostino. Riccardo Sanguigni was beheaded here in 1406 by Paolo Orsini for siding with the Colonna.

places.name: Fontana di piazza San Simeone
places.address: Piazzetta di San Simeone, 00186 Roma RM
places.summary: A small fountain on the piazzetta di San Simeone, which Roma Capitale's street register records as lying in Ponte alone.
places.history: it.wikipedia records that the fountain is sixteenth-century in origin, made in the works that branched the Acqua Felice conduit, and that it was definitively placed in this square in 1973. It stood originally in piazza Montanara, in front of the Theatre of Marcellus.

places.name: Monumento a Nicola Spedalieri
places.summary: A bronze monument on piazza Sforza Cesarini, which Roma Capitale's street register records as lying in Ponte alone.
places.history: it.wikipedia's article on the rione records the monument as a bronze by Mario Rutelli, made between 1898 and 1900.

places.name: Ponte Vittorio Emanuele II
places.summary: The bridge from piazza Pasquale Paoli to lungotevere Vaticano, carrying road traffic toward the Vatican side. It lies in two rioni, Ponte and Borgo. it.wikipedia records that its official name has been Ponte Vittorio Emanuele Secondo since 2015.
places.history: it.wikipedia records that Ennio De Rossi designed the bridge in 1886, that it was named before it was built, and that work was interrupted and resumed in 1908. Roma Capitale records that it was first inaugurated on 5 June 1911, for the fiftieth anniversary of Italian unification, and inaugurated again on 28 April 1912, when the sculptural groups were finally placed.

places.name: Ponte Umberto I
places.summary: The bridge from piazza di Ponte Umberto I to piazza dei Tribunali. It lies in two rioni, Ponte and Prati.
places.history: it.wikipedia records that Angelo Vescovali designed the bridge, that it was built between 1885 and 1895 and dedicated to Umberto I, who inaugurated it with Queen Margherita. It has three masonry arches faced in travertine and Subiaco stone and is about 106 metres long.

places.name: Ponte Neroniano
places.summary: The remains of the Neronian or Triumphal bridge, which carried the ancient Via Triumphalis across the Tiber. A pier stub survives in the river.
places.history: it.wikipedia records that the bridge was built under Nero in the first century to improve links with his property on the right bank, including his mother Agrippina's villa, and that an attribution to Caligula has also been argued. The date of its destruction is unknown; it may have gone out of use when the Aurelian Walls were built.

entries.name: Ponte Sant'Angelo
entries.note: The bridge the rione is named and blazoned for, built by Hadrian in 136 AD as the pons Aelius and given ten angels bearing the symbols of the Passion in 1668.

entries.name: Museo Nazionale Romano - Palazzo Altemps
entries.note: A Renaissance palace raised in 1477 for Girolamo Riario, now one of the four sites of the Museo Nazionale Romano; Tuesday to Sunday 09.30 to 19.00, last admission 18.00.

entries.name: Chiesa di Santa Maria della Pace
entries.note: Pietro da Cortona's convex front of 1656 for Alexander VII, over a church named for the Peace of Bagnolo, with Raphael's Sibyls and angels of 1514 on the chapel arch.

entries.name: Chiostro del Bramante
entries.note: Bramante's cloister of 1500 to 1504 for the adjoining church, an exhibition venue since 1996; hours change with the show, so check chiostrodelbramante.it.

entries.name: Chiesa di Santa Maria dell'Anima
entries.note: The German-speaking community's national church, consecrated in 1542, holding the funerary monument of Pope Adrian VI made between 1524 and 1527.

entries.name: Via dei Coronari
entries.note: About 500 metres straight through the rione, once called Via Recta, named for the sellers of rosaries who set up shop along the pilgrims' route toward St Peter's.

entries.name: Basilica di San Giovanni Battista dei Fiorentini
entries.note: The Florentine national church at the head of via Giulia, from a competition Leo X held in 1518, with Alessandro Galilei's travertine front of 1734; Borromini and Maderno are buried here.

entries.name: Oratorio del Gonfalone
entries.note: Built between 1544 and 1547 for the Arciconfraternita del Gonfalone, with a Passion cycle in twelve episodes painted from 1569 to 1576; visits are arranged through the contacts Roma Capitale gives.

entries.name: Museo Napoleonico
entries.note: Count Giuseppe Primoli's Napoleonic collection, given to the city in 1927 and shown in his rebuilt palace; Tuesday to Sunday 10.00 to 18.00, last entry 17.15.

entries.name: Musei di San Salvatore in Lauro
entries.note: The Pio Sodalizio dei Piceni's galleries, holding the permanent donations of Emilio Greco and Umberto Mastroianni; Tuesday to Saturday 10.00 to 13.00 and 16.00 to 19.00.

entries.name: Basilica dei Santi Celso e Giuliano in Banchi
entries.note: The church of the banking quarter, consecrated in 432 and made a papal chapel by Innocent III in 1198; it opens 07.00 to 12.00 and 15.00 to 19.00 on weekdays.

entries.name: Tor Sanguigna
entries.note: What survives of the Sanguigni stronghold, where Riccardo Sanguigni was beheaded in 1406 by Paolo Orsini for siding with the Colonna.

entries.name: Piazza di Ponte Sant'Angelo
entries.note: The square at the left-bank bridgehead, where the rione's article records that condemned prisoners were led in procession and a gallows stood.

entries.name: Ponte Neroniano
entries.note: A pier stub in the river, all that is left of the bridge built under Nero to carry the Via Triumphalis to the right bank.

links.note: Ponte Sant'Angelo and Ponte Vittorio Emanuele II each lie in Ponte and in Borgo, where Ponte Sant'Angelo meets Castel Sant'Angelo.
Ponte's landward neighbour. Roma Capitale's register puts piazza Navona wholly in Parione, and several streets behind it in both rioni.
Ponte Umberto I crosses into Prati, which holds three further Tiber bridges of its own.
The three-day Rome itinerary in this series, which crosses Ponte Sant'Angelo on its way to the Vatican.
